course.title: Digital Marketing
course.description: A hands-on tour of how businesses attract, convert, and keep customers online — the funnel, SEO, paid ads, email, social, and analytics. Topics mirror the foundations of the Google Digital Marketing & E-commerce Certificate; it targets digital-marketing-certificate-style foundations with original prose and vendor-neutral concepts.

questions.prompt: The top of the marketing funnel is mainly about…
questions.explanation: The funnel runs awareness → consideration → conversion → retention; the top is awareness — see 'The funnel and channels'.

questions.prompt: SEO is best described as improving…
questions.explanation: SEO earns organic, unpaid search traffic — see 'SEO & content'.

questions.prompt: ROAS is calculated as…
questions.explanation: Return on ad spend = revenue ÷ ad spend — see 'Paid ads'.

questions.prompt: CPC stands for…
questions.explanation: CPC = cost per click = spend ÷ clicks — see 'Paid ads'.

questions.prompt: An email open rate is opens divided by…
questions.explanation: Open rate uses delivered emails, not sent — see 'Email marketing'.

questions.prompt: The point of an A/B test is to…
options: compare two versions to see which performs better
questions.explanation: A/B testing isolates one change and measures the difference — see 'Analytics'.

questions.prompt: 'Paid social' refers to…
questions.explanation: Paid social is buying ad placements on social platforms — see 'Paid ads'.

questions.prompt: Attribution answers the question…
options: how much did the ad cost
which touchpoints get credit for a conversion
how many people opened the email
questions.explanation: Attribution assigns credit across the touchpoints on the path to conversion — see 'Analytics'.

lessons.title: The digital marketing funnel and channels
lessons.grammar_note: Funnel order: awareness → consideration → conversion → retention.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Name the stages of the marketing funnel and match common channels to each stage. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, which stage sits at the *top* of the funnel?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A *funnel* describes how a large audience narrows into a few paying customers: *awareness* (they first hear of you), *consideration* (they compare options), *conversion* (they buy), and *retention* (they stay and repeat). Channels are the paths you use: *owned* (your site, email list), *earned* (SEO rankings, word of mouth, press), and *paid* (search ads, social ads). No single channel fills the whole funnel — awareness channels feed the top, while email and retargeting do the closing work near the bottom.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: A campaign reaches 10,000 people. 5% click through to the site → 500 visits. Of those, 20% leave an email (become leads) → 100 leads. 10% of leads buy → 10 customers. End-to-end conversion is 10 ÷ 10,000 = 0.1%. Notice each stage multiplies: lift the visit-to-lead rate from 20% to 30% and you'd get 150 leads and ~15 customers from the same 10,000 reach — a 50% gain with no extra ad spend.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Label the funnel stage for each: (1) a first-time viewer watches a brand video, (2) a shopper reads three comparison reviews, (3) a visitor completes checkout, (4) a buyer opens a 'how to get started' email a week later. Answers: (1) awareness, (2) consideration, (3) conversion, (4) retention.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: pouring all budget into awareness while nothing captures or closes the interest it creates. Mistake: treating 'traffic' as a goal instead of a means. Exit: (a) Which stage does an email welcome series mainly serve? (b) Is your own website an owned, earned, or paid channel? Answers: retention (and conversion); owned.

lessons.title: SEO and content marketing
lessons.grammar_note: SEO = organic (unpaid); SEM/ads = paid. Keep them separate.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain how search engine optimization earns organic traffic and how content supports it. Warm-up: does SEO buy placement, or earn it?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: *SEO* is the practice of making pages easier for search engines to find, understand, and rank so they appear in *organic* (unpaid) results. It rests on three pillars: *technical* (a crawlable, fast, mobile-friendly site), *on-page* (useful content matching what people search — the *keyword* intent — plus clear titles and headings), and *off-page* (credible links and mentions that signal trust). *Content marketing* feeds SEO: helpful articles, guides, and answers that match real questions attract links and rank over time. Two metrics matter here — *impressions* (how often your page shows in results) and *search CTR* (clicks ÷ impressions).

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: A guide shows in search 20,000 times in a month (impressions) and earns 600 clicks. Search CTR = 600 ÷ 20,000 = 3%. You improve the title and internal links and the page climbs from position 6 to position 3, where CTR roughly doubles to ~6%. With the same 20,000 impressions that's about 1,200 clicks — double the organic traffic with zero ad spend. If 2% of those visitors convert, you go from 12 to 24 conversions.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Classify each as technical, on-page, or off-page SEO: (1) compressing images so pages load faster, (2) writing a title that matches the search phrase, (3) earning a link from an industry blog, (4) fixing broken redirects. Answers: (1) technical, (2) on-page, (3) off-page, (4) technical.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: 'keyword stuffing' — cramming terms unnaturally; modern search rewards genuinely useful content that satisfies intent. Mistake: confusing SEO (organic) with paid search ads. Exit: (a) A page with 15,000 impressions and 450 clicks has what search CTR? (b) Is a backlink on-page or off-page? Answers: 450 ÷ 15,000 = 3%; off-page.

lessons.title: Paid ads: search, social, and the metrics
lessons.grammar_note: CTR = clicks/impressions; CPC = spend/clicks; ROAS = revenue/spend.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Read a paid campaign's core metrics and compute CTR, CPC, CPM, conversion rate, CPA, and ROAS. Warm-up: what does ROAS divide by what?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: *Paid ads* buy placement on search engines (*paid search*, where you bid on keywords) and inside social feeds (*paid social*, where you target audiences). You usually pay per click (*CPC*) or per thousand impressions (*CPM*). The metrics chain together: *CTR* = clicks ÷ impressions measures how compelling the ad is; *conversion rate* = conversions ÷ clicks measures how well the landing page closes; *CPA* = spend ÷ conversions is what each customer costs; and *ROAS* = revenue ÷ ad spend tells you whether the whole thing pays. A campaign can have a great CTR and still lose money if the conversion rate is low.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: A search campaign gets 100,000 impressions and 2,000 clicks, so CTR = 2,000 ÷ 100,000 = 2%. Ad spend is $1,000, so CPC = $1,000 ÷ 2,000 = $0.50 and CPM = ($1,000 ÷ 100,000) × 1,000 = $10. Those clicks produce 100 sales, so conversion rate = 100 ÷ 2,000 = 5% and CPA = $1,000 ÷ 100 = $10. The sales bring $5,000 in revenue, so ROAS = $5,000 ÷ $1,000 = 5 (a 5:1 return, or 500%). Because each $10 customer is worth $50 in revenue, scaling this spend is justified.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: A social ad has 40,000 impressions, 800 clicks, $400 spend, 20 conversions, and $1,600 revenue. Compute: (1) CTR, (2) CPC, (3) conversion rate, (4) CPA, (5) ROAS. Answers: (1) 800 ÷ 40,000 = 2%, (2) $400 ÷ 800 = $0.50, (3) 20 ÷ 800 = 2.5%, (4) $400 ÷ 20 = $20, (5) $1,600 ÷ $400 = 4 (4:1).

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: chasing a low CPC while ignoring conversion rate — cheap clicks that never buy still waste budget. Mistake: reading ROAS of 4 as '4% return'; it means $4 back per $1 spent. Exit: (a) Spend $250 for 25 conversions — what's the CPA? (b) $900 revenue on $300 spend — what's the ROAS? Answers: $250 ÷ 25 = $10; $900 ÷ $300 = 3 (3:1).

questions.prompt: The funnel stage where shoppers compare options is…
questions.explanation: Consideration sits between awareness and the purchase.

questions.prompt: A page shows 20,000 times and earns 600 clicks. Its search CTR is…
Earning a link from another site is which kind of SEO?
questions.explanation: Links and mentions are off-page signals.

questions.prompt: $1,000 spend and 2,000 clicks gives a CPC of…
A campaign returns $5,000 on $1,000 spend. ROAS is…
100 conversions from 2,000 clicks is a conversion rate of…

lessons.title: Email marketing and automation
lessons.grammar_note: Open rate and click rate both use *delivered* emails as the base.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe how email marketing works, set up a basic automated flow, and compute open and click rates. Warm-up: which number is the base for an open rate — sent or delivered?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: *Email marketing* sends messages to a list you own — the highest-control, lowest-cost channel, because you're not renting the audience. It splits into *broadcasts* (one-off sends, like a newsletter) and *automation* (*flows* triggered by behavior: a welcome series when someone subscribes, a cart-abandonment reminder, a re-engagement nudge). Key metrics use *delivered* emails as the base: *open rate* = opens ÷ delivered, *click rate* = clicks ÷ delivered, and *click-to-open rate* = clicks ÷ opens. *Segmentation* — sending to the right slice of the list — lifts every one of them. A permission-based list and an easy unsubscribe keep you both effective and compliant.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: You send 10,000 emails; 200 bounce, so 9,800 are delivered. 2,940 people open → open rate = 2,940 ÷ 9,800 = 30%. 490 click → click rate = 490 ÷ 9,800 = 5%, and click-to-open = 490 ÷ 2,940 ≈ 16.7%. Now you segment: sending only to the 3,000 most-engaged subscribers lifts the open rate to 45% and the click rate to 9%. Fewer emails, more clicks — automation applied to the right segment beats a bigger blast.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: From 5,000 delivered emails you get 1,500 opens and 300 clicks. Compute: (1) open rate, (2) click rate, (3) click-to-open rate. Also (4): name the trigger for a cart-abandonment flow. Answers: (1) 1,500 ÷ 5,000 = 30%, (2) 300 ÷ 5,000 = 6%, (3) 300 ÷ 1,500 = 20%, (4) a shopper adds items but leaves without buying.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: buying email lists — it tanks deliverability and trust; grow permission-based lists instead. Mistake: dividing opens by emails *sent* rather than *delivered*. Exit: (a) 4,000 delivered, 1,200 opens — open rate? (b) Is a welcome series a broadcast or an automation? Answers: 1,200 ÷ 4,000 = 30%; an automation.

lessons.title: Analytics and measurement
lessons.grammar_note: A KPI is a metric tied to a goal; not every metric is a KPI.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Choose meaningful KPIs, read basic attribution, and interpret an A/B test. Warm-up: what makes a metric a KPI rather than just a number?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: *Analytics* turns activity into decisions. A *KPI* (key performance indicator) is a metric tied to a goal — conversion rate and CPA are KPIs; raw pageviews usually aren't. *Attribution* decides which touchpoints get credit when a customer takes several steps before buying: *last-click* gives all credit to the final touch, *first-click* to the first, and *multi-touch* splits it across the path. Different models tell different stories about which channel 'worked'. *A/B testing* isolates one change (a headline, a button) by splitting traffic between version A and version B and comparing a single KPI, so you improve based on evidence rather than opinion.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: You A/B test a landing page. Version A: 1,000 visitors, 40 conversions → 4.0% conversion rate. Version B (new headline): 1,000 visitors, 50 conversions → 5.0%. The absolute lift is 1 percentage point; the *relative* lift is (5 − 4) ÷ 4 = 25%. Now attribution: a buyer clicked a search ad, later an email, then converted. Last-click credits the email; first-click credits the search ad — same sale, two different stories, which is why you pick a model on purpose before judging channels.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: (1) Version A converts 30 of 600 visitors; version B converts 48 of 600 — give both conversion rates and the relative lift. (2) Under last-click attribution, which touch gets credit: a shopper sees a social ad, then clicks an email, then buys? Answers: (1) A = 30 ÷ 600 = 5%, B = 48 ÷ 600 = 8%, relative lift = (8 − 5) ÷ 5 = 60%; (2) the email (the last click before purchase).

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating a 4%→5% result as '1% better' — it's a 25% relative lift. Mistake: calling every dashboard number a KPI. Mistake: ending an A/B test too early on too little traffic. Exit: (a) 20 conversions from 500 visitors is what rate? (b) Which model gives all credit to the final touch? Answers: 20 ÷ 500 = 4%; last-click.

lessons.title: Applied project: build a digital marketing plan

sections.heading: The task
sections.text: Pick one real or imagined product and write a one-page digital marketing plan for it. You won't run the campaign — you'll design it so the channels, budget, and KPIs fit together.

sections.heading: Milestones
sections.text: 1) Describe the product and its target customer in two sentences. 2) Map at least one channel to each funnel stage (awareness, consideration, conversion, retention) and say why. 3) Set a monthly budget and split it across channels (percentages that sum to 100%). 4) Define 3–4 KPIs with target numbers (e.g. target CPA, target ROAS, email open rate, organic CTR). 5) Name one A/B test you'd run first and the single metric it would judge.

sections.heading: Self-check rubric
sections.text: ✔ Every funnel stage has at least one channel. ✔ The budget split sums to 100% and matches your priorities. ✔ Each KPI is measurable and has a target number, not just a name. ✔ Your ROAS/CPA targets are internally consistent (if a customer is worth $50, a $60 target CPA loses money). ✔ The A/B test changes one thing and names one metric. If all five hold, your plan is coherent enough to brief a team.
